title: SDK Experimentation Labs and Issue Resolver Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview
--------
This page describes the SDK Experimentation Labs program and the associated Issue Resolver Playbook used by Developer Experience (DevX) to onboard new SDK patterns, validate API examples, and reduce repetitive support escalations. The goal is to make safe, fast iteration on SDK features while producing reproducible canonical fixes for the support team and docs site.

Audience
--------
- SDK engineers and maintainers
- Developer advocates and technical writers
- Support engineers and on-call devx leads

What the labs deliver
---------------------
- Reproducible quickstarts and minimal sample apps for each SDK surface (generation, streaming, embeddings, batching).
- A canonical-fixes catalog: triaged patterns + root cause + validated patch.
- A docs-site lifecycle that ensures snippet parity between README, quickstart, and docs rendering.
- A short feedback loop from support issues to SDK tests and docs changes.

Program structure
-----------------
1. Lab intake: maintainers file a lab request when a new API surface or model variant is introduced. Include: rationale, target customers, API contract, and telemetry flags to collect.
2. Authoring: SDK author pairs with a tech writer to produce: minimal quickstart, two API examples, and an integration test harness.
3. Validation: run the examples across local emulation and a CI lab against the runtime staging cluster and with a small set of live model variants.
4. Publish: merge artifacts into the docs site and the SDK repo. Tag the quickstart with a canonical-fix id if it closed a support pattern.

Quickstarts and templates catalog (summary table)
------------------------------------------------
Name | Purpose | Minimum deliverables | Owner
-----|---------|----------------------|------
sdk-experimentation-template | Fast scaffold for new SDK features | README, quickstart app, CI job, telemetry knobs | SDK author team
sample-embed-to-gen | Show embedding-driven retrieval + generation | sample app, test dataset, golden traces | Integrations team

(Avoid copy/paste: actual catalog is a living Confluence table; link in related_pages above.)

Authoring guidelines (checklist)
--------------------------------
- Keep quickstarts under 200 lines of code.
- Include a network/emulation mode for offline devs (see example below).
- Provide an explicit "expected output" golden trace for every example.
- Add a short troubleshooting section with at least one likely symptom and a reproducible command.

Example: minimal streaming quickstart (pseudo-code)
--------------------------------------------------
# Python pseudocode example (should be embedded on docs site in fenced code block)
from redwood_sdk import Client
client = Client(api_key="${REDWOOD_API_KEY}")
with client.stream("gpt-4o-mini") as stream:
    stream.send({"role":"user","content":"Write a haiku about compilers"})
    for chunk in stream.recv_chunks():
        print(chunk.text, end="")

Dev note: Add a test that asserts concatenated chunks == golden_output.

Docs site operating procedures
------------------------------
- Branching: all quickstarts live in docs-source/quickstarts. Changes must include a generated snippet diff via the docs CI preview job.
- Canary publishing: new quickstarts are published to the staging docs site under /labs/ for 72 hours. During canary window, telemetry is collected (snippet usage, example run failures, runtime error rates).
- Ownership: each quickstart must include a two-line metadata header: maintainer, last-verified-date, and supported SDK versions.
- Snippet canonicalization: snippets in SDK READMEs are the canonical source. Docs site build pulls snippets from those files rather than inlining long copy. This reduces drift.

CI and test requirements for lab merges
--------------------------------------
- Unit tests covering API contract surface (>= 90% contract assertions).
- Integration harness that runs the quickstart end-to-end in emulation and reports a golden-trace hash.
- Telemetry smoke: example should emit at least these telemetry events: example.start, example.success/failure, example.latency_ms.
- Docs preview: docs CI must show snippet diffs and render warnings if a code block exceeds 200 lines.

Top support issues and canonical fixes (summary)
------------------------------------------------
1) Symptom: streaming partials drop order in some consumers.
   - Root cause: client code concatenates chunks without respecting 'sequence_id' emitted by runtime when multiplexing multiple streams on the same connection.
   - Canonical fix: use stream.recv_chunks(order_by='sequence_id') helper or enable "ordered_streaming": true in client config.
   - Playbook steps:
     1. Reproduce with the failing snippet in the lab emulation mode (run reproduce_stream_drop.sh).
     2. Patch the example to use ordered recv helper.
     3. Add regression test that interleaves 5 concurrent streams and asserts ordering.
     4. Publish fix and cross-link support ticket with canonical-fix id CF-2027-014.

2) Symptom: embedding indexes return inconsistent distances after SDK update.
   - Root cause: SDK float32->float16 conversion was applied at client-side before normalization step, causing small numerical drift for low-norm vectors.
   - Canonical fix: move quantization to server-side and document the versioned vector schema in quickstart.
   - Playbook steps: see repository patch in sample-embed-to-gen quickstart; add an end-to-end golden trace to catch drift.

3) Symptom: elevated error-rate for ephemeral tokens in CI.
   - Root cause: token provider rotated keys mid-run without propagating the new token to ephemeral test runners.
   - Canonical fix: add a token refresh hook to the test harness and a CI gating step that ensures all ephemeral runners have token_version == latest.

Triage runbook (short)
----------------------
1. Capture: request telemetry id from support ticket and copy the golden-trace id.
2. Reproduce: clone the associated quickstart and run in emulation mode: ./dev/run_emulation.sh --trace ${ID}
3. Isolate: toggle SDK feature flags to find the minimal repro.
4. Patch: create minimal PR in sdk/ with test and example fix.
5. Verify: run canary docs preview + CI lab.
6. Ship: merge, publish docs, add note to the support ticket, and mark canonical-fix label.

Metrics and success signals
--------------------------
- Reduction in "same root cause" tickets for SDK surfaces by 60% within 90 days of lab adoption.
- Mean time to publish a canonical fix: target <= 7 days from first support ticket.
- Snippet drift: target < 2% of quickstarts per quarter requiring emergency patch.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
-------------------------------------
- Emulation local run:
  export REDWOOD_EMULATE=1
  ./dev/run_example.sh --example quickstarts/sample-embed-to-gen

- Golden trace check (CI):
  python tools/compare_traces.py --expected traces/golden.hash --actual traces/latest.hash

- Create a canonical-fix PR template (example title):
  [CF-<id>] fix: streaming-order-preservation in python-sdk quickstart

Ownership and escalation contacts
--------------------------------
- DevX on-call: devx-oncall@redwood.ai
- SDK authors: see quickstart metadata header (maintainer)
- Docs site owner: Marco Chen (docs-infra)

Notes and future work
---------------------
- Plan to add a lightweight sandbox runner that spins up a tenant-scoped runtime for higher-fidelity validation.
- Investigate automated snippet linting that validates both syntax and golden-trace equivalence during PR reviews.

If you are proposing a new lab, copy the SDK Experimentation template and complete the intake form attached to this page, then tag @devx-oncall for review.
